title: MCA Factor Rate vs APR: How to Compare Financing Costs
excerpt: Compare factor rate, estimated APR, and effective annual rate using payment timing, net proceeds, fees, and reproducible worked examples.
author: Business Debt Insider
contentMd:
A factor rate tells you the contractual payback relative to an advance. It does not tell you the annualized financing cost. To estimate that cost, you also need the amount actually received, each payment amount, and when the payments occur.

**Editorial correction — October 11, 2026:** We replaced the previous approximate APR examples and removed unsupported claims about typical rates, borrower behavior, and settlement outcomes. The examples below use the same equal-payment method as our [APR calculator](/tools/apr-calculator).

## The four numbers to keep separate

| Measure | What it describes | What it leaves out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Factor rate | Total scheduled payback divided by the stated advance | Fees deducted at funding and the timing of repayment |
| Dollar financing cost | Total payments minus net proceeds received | How long the capital is available |
| Estimated APR | Periodic cash-flow rate multiplied by periods per year | Compounding within the year |
| Effective annual rate | The periodic rate compounded over a year | Your actual dollar cost if the agreement lasts less than a year |

An estimated APR is a comparison measure under stated assumptions. It is not automatically the APR required by a particular commercial-financing disclosure law. The applicable calculation and disclosure requirements depend on the product and jurisdiction.

## Start with net proceeds

Suppose the stated advance is $100,000 and $3,000 is deducted at funding. The business receives $97,000. If scheduled payments total $145,000, the cash cost is $48,000 relative to the amount received. Using $100,000 as the usable proceeds would understate that cost.

Record deductions separately from amounts sent to an existing creditor. A refinance payoff is not automatically a fee: understand what obligation was discharged and avoid counting the same financing cost twice. If cash flows are complicated, an equal-payment calculator may not represent the transaction adequately.

## How the calculator works

The calculator solves for a periodic rate that makes the present value of all scheduled payments equal to net proceeds. For equal payments at the end of each period, the relationship is:

`net proceeds = payment × [1 − (1 + periodic rate)^(-number of payments)] / periodic rate`

It then multiplies that periodic rate by `365 / days between payments` to estimate a nominal annual percentage rate. The effective annual rate instead uses `(1 + periodic rate)^(365 / days between payments) − 1`.

The [CFPB's explanation of APR determination](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/interp-22/) provides background on actuarial calculations. That consumer-credit reference does not establish which disclosure rules apply to a particular MCA.

## Worked examples you can reproduce

These are hypothetical schedules, not quotes, typical market rates, or predictions about your agreement. They assume equal payments, the first payment one full period after funding, and a 365-day year.

| Input or result | Example A | Example B | Example C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stated advance | $100,000 | $50,000 | $100,000 |
| Upfront fees | $0 | $0 | $3,000 |
| Net proceeds | $100,000 | $50,000 | $97,000 |
| Total scheduled payback | $145,000 | $65,000 | $145,000 |
| Payment schedule | 26 weekly payments | 52 weekly payments | 26 weekly payments |
| Payment amount | $5,576.92* | $1,250.00 | $5,576.92* |
| Factor rate | 1.45 | 1.30 | 1.45 |
| Dollar cost | $45,000 | $15,000 | $48,000 |
| Estimated APR | 155.1% | 54.3% | 168.9% |
| Effective annual rate | 360.9% | 71.6% | 427.3% |

*The calculation uses the unrounded payment amount; the displayed amount is rounded to cents. Twenty-six weekly periods equal 182 days and 52 equal 364 days. The effective annual rate is a compounded annual comparison, not an additional bill or the percentage of the advance you actually pay over those shorter periods.*

Example C shows why fees matter: the payment schedule is unchanged from A, but the business receives less money at the beginning.

## Why a simple annualization gives a different answer

In Example A, dividing the $45,000 cost by $100,000 and scaling 182 days to one year gives about 90.2%. This simple annualized cost does not account for the balance being returned throughout the term. It is not the cash-flow APR estimate of 155.1%.

Do not use a fixed multiplier to convert factor rate into APR. The result changes with the exact payment schedule, deductions, and first-payment date. Monthly loans also have repayment timing; that issue is not unique to MCAs.

## When the estimate does not fit your contract

Our tool models daily calendar payments or payments every seven days. It does not model weekday-only withdrawals, bank holidays, irregular payment dates, variable remittances based on actual sales, payment pauses, or every commercial-disclosure convention.

If a payment amount changes, rebuild the cash-flow schedule. If a revenue purchase has an uncertain duration, a fixed schedule is a scenario rather than a known term. Review the signed agreement and applicable disclosures alongside the calculation. [California DFPI's commercial-financing disclosure information](https://dfpi.ca.gov/regulated-industries/california-financing-law/about-california-financing-law/california-financing-law-commercial-financing-disclosures/) is one starting point for that jurisdiction.

## What the number can and cannot establish

Annualized cost helps compare offers, spot omitted fees, and explain why a lower payment may still cost more overall. It does not by itself establish that a contract is unlawful, unenforceable, or eligible for a settlement discount. Those questions require the agreement, facts, and applicable law.

Before a review, assemble the funding statement, payment schedule, fee breakdown, and any amendments. Use the [calculator](/tools/apr-calculator) for a clearly labeled estimate, then use the [lender guides](/lenders) to identify the relevant product and servicing questions.
